name: STATIS multi-table analysis
title: Did the whole stress-test–payout pattern change after 2020?
what: Treats each test year as a table, scores how alike the years' correlation patterns are, and maps years and variables together.
pick_line: Reliability-corrected RV so single odd years can be tested; must be unbiased within ±0.01 in simulation.
data: Public filings (Fed DFAST results, FR Y-9C); descriptive only
one: The joint stress–payout pattern splits into 2013–19 and 2020–25 eras; no single correlation shows it.

picture.la: Usual tool: one correlation per year (noisy)
picture.lb: STATIS: whole-pattern similarity peaks at a 2021 cut

findings.h: The whole correlation pattern splits into a pre-2020 and a 2020+ era.
findings.t: Across 13 exercises (2013–2025) and 7 variables, years in the same era are more alike than years in different eras: within − between RV = 0.0108, exact permutation p = 0.023 (rank 39 of all 1,716 ways to pick six 'after' years). Modified RV: p = 0.016; without double-centring: p = 0.019.
findings.note: Exploratory: among contiguous cuts the gap is largest when the 'after' era starts in 2021 (0.015), the first year with a stress capital buffer in force. That cut was not pre-registered. Years' sample sizes do not drive it (Spearman 0.19 between RV-to-compromise and firm count, p = 0.53).

findings.h: No single correlation change explains it.
findings.t: Of 21 variable pairs, the largest era change is CET1 drawdown ~ SA loan losses (Spearman −0.05 → +0.19; pair p = 0.009, familywise max-T p = 0.11). Payout/RWA ~ drawdown, the usual check, goes −0.24 → −0.37 (p = 0.10, max-T 0.92). Payout ~ net buybacks loosens 0.87 → 0.71 (p = 0.030, max-T 0.75).
findings.note: Read as: many small moves in the same direction add up to a significant whole-pattern shift that no one-pair test sees. Era means are of yearly Spearman correlations; exact permutation over 1,716 era splits.

chart.title: Era change in Spearman ρ (after − before)

findings.h: The split is moderate, not robust.
findings.t: Dropping one exercise at a time, the era test stays below 0.05 in 9 of 13 cases; dropping 2015, 2016, 2021 or 2022 pushes p to 0.057–0.089.

chart.title: Era-split p, leave one year out

findings.h: Our 'which single year departs' check failed: RV's small-sample bias.
findings.t: The pre-registered firm-bootstrap rule flagged 2013, 2019, 2022 and 2025. But in 6 of 13 years the observed RV to the compromise lies above its own bootstrap 97.5% bound: resampling 18–35 firms adds noise that lowers RV, so the bands are shifted down and the rule is not valid.
findings.note: This is the known RV bias (Smilde et al. 2009). The Math avenue (top pick) is a bias-corrected RV.

chart.title: Years with observed RV above its own band

findings.h: Firm paths: who moves in the joint stress–payout space.
findings.t: Partial triadic analysis on the 21 firms in every test 2022–25: the longest paths are Barclays US, Charles Schwab, UBS Americas and State Street. Path length tracks payout-rank changes only weakly (Spearman 0.11; 0.45 for the 28 firms in every test 2015–18).
findings.note: So in recent years firms move mostly on the stress side (drawdown, losses, capital), not on payouts. Descriptive; firm paths use public data only.
